1.pericope_label: Why, seeing times are not hidden from the Almighty, do they that know him not see his days; some remove the landmarks and violently take away flocks, they drive away the ass of the fatherless and take the widow ox for a pledge, and turn the needy out of the way

schools.summary: Gill explains the landmarks as the stones anciently set to distinguish one man ground from another, removed either secretly by night or openly by men with power enough to pretend they were wrongly placed, and notes that the heathen too had a Jupiter of boundaries whose stones a remover was slain for touching; he takes the ass of the fatherless as the single beast of a man who had no friend to provide for him, which made the taking of it the more inhuman, and reads the turning of the needy out of the way either of their livelihood, by the taking of what they lived by, or literally out of the road, pushed aside by a haughty man or avoiding him for fear.

Henry grants the premise of the opening question in three parts, that past times are not hidden from God judgment, present times from his providence, nor future times from his prescience, and draws the consequence that if wicked men die unpunished we cannot say they escaped him by surprise, since he foresaw it and even ordered it; Job asserts the omniscience first, he notes, as other prophets in like straits asserted the righteousness or the holiness or the goodness of God, because general truths must be held fast even where particular events cannot be reconciled to them; and he sets the whole catalogue under the head of tyranny, wrong done under pretence of law and authority, with the tears of the oppressed unregarded and power on the side of the oppressors, adding that forging or destroying deeds is now the crime equivalent to moving a landmark.

Clarke prefers an emendation that turns the opening question into a wish, that the Almighty would keep set days of doom, as courts keep term times, so that an accused man might look forward to one; he gives the moving of the landmark its motive, that the posts were shifted onto a neighbour ground so that by contracting his boundaries a man might enlarge his own, reports two other readings of the next clause, one making the verb destroy rather than feed and one in which the Greek had read shepherd, so that both are carried off together, and turns the closed path into a case from his own country, where a nobleman shut up an ancient footway and a cobbler took him to law and won it, answering those who wondered at his boldness that he did not like to leave the world worse than he found it; Wesley keeps the last of the three senses of turning the needy aside, that they labour to keep out of the path where these oppressors walk and hide themselves for fear of further injury, and glosses the pledge taken as against the law written first in men hearts and afterwards in Scripture.

Ellicott reads the opening verse as a general perplexity rather than a private one, arising from a survey of God dealings with the world, and observes that the second negative is so placed in our version as to make the line ambiguous, which would be cured by reading see not instead of not see; he notes that the ass and the ox are named singly because the fatherless and the widow had no more than one, that the oppression described is first of the country and then of the city, and that behind it we seem to catch a glimpse of some abject and servile race haunting the desert and suffering at the hands of stronger tribes; Keil and Delitzsch supply their own rendering of the four verses, the landmarks removed, the flocks stolen and pastured, the orphan ass carried off and the widow ox distrained, and the poor of the land obliged to slink away together.

debates.question: What is the opening question asking for?

sides.position: why the godly do not see God day of judgment, the delay being a mystery of providence with a reason we shall know later
why God does not keep set days of doom, as courts keep term times, so that an accused man might look forward to one
why those who know God are as perplexed about his government as those who do not, the question arising from a survey of the world

debates.question: Who is turned out of the way, and how?

sides.position: the needy, driven from their livelihood or literally pushed off the road by a haughty man
the poor, who keep out of the oppressors path and hide for fear of further injury
a subject and servile race, barred from the paths they had used time out of mind

outliers: Clarke alone brings a lawsuit from his own country, a cobbler against a nobleman over a closed footpath, to illustrate the stopping of an ancient way.
Henry alone makes the opening verse a lesson in method, that the general truth of God omniscience must be held fast before the particular difficulty is examined.
themes: a question about delay, not about knowledge
boundary stones moved by night
the one beast of a fatherless child
an ancient path closed against the poor

5.pericope_label: As wild asses in the desert they go forth to their work rising betimes for a prey; they reap the field and gather the vintage of the wicked, they cause the naked to lodge without clothing, they pluck the fatherless from the breast, they make oil within their walls and suffer thirst, and men groan out of the city

schools.summary: Gill allows the comparison of the wild asses to be dropped and the words taken literally of the beasts whose proper place is the wilderness, though he follows the Targum in supplying the note of similitude; he holds that the wicked reap the standing corn of the poor so impudently that they do not trouble to steal it from the barn, explains that those called naked are not wholly so but thinly clad, and that even their bed clothes are taken so that they must lie all night with nothing over them, and that lying at the foot of a hill, where the clouds gather and break or the snow melts in the heat of the day, they are drenched by the streams that run down; he reads the plucking of the fatherless either as a design to starve the child, or to sell it into slavery, or to force the mother to wean it early so that she could be put to work.

Henry presses the charge against employers, that they not only give no wages, though the labourer is worthy of his hire, but will not so much as give meat and drink, so that those who carry the sheaves are hungry and those who tread the winepresses suffer thirst, which he calls worse than muzzling the ox that treads out the corn; such masters, he adds, forget that they have a Master in heaven.

Clarke reads the opening verse of a predatory life, men who roam the wilderness and seize whatever they find and so support themselves and their families, and keeps to those roaming hordes on the next, who carry off grain and olives and vines in a sudden irruption and plunge with the spoil into the desert where none can follow; he defends the mountain showers against an emendation that would make them torrents, having seen in mountainous country the tail of a water-spout break and pour out what would be incredible to anyone who had not watched it, reads the whole description as characteristic of a wandering people, ill fed, ill clothed and often without even tents, who can carry no household stuff because they may have to fly for their lives, takes the plucking of the fatherless of children seized to be brought up in slavery, and makes the pledge the exaction of an oppressive landlord who lets his ground at an exorbitant rent and then takes the labourer cow or cart or bed when he cannot pay it; and he reports from his own experience of surveying a poor district of a great city that every dwelling was full of people and the poor not only badly fed and clothed but wretchedly lodged; Wesley makes the wild asses a figure for the oppressors themselves, lawless and fierce and greedy of prey, who go out to spoil and rob, holds that these robbers plundered promiscuously, even their own brethren in iniquity, and reads the cry of the last verse as the blood of men wounded to death calling aloud to God for vengeance.

Ellicott takes the reaping the opposite way from Gill, that the poor reap the tyrant corn and cut his provender and go without themselves, marks the turn at the last verse of the span, where the survey moves inside the city walls, and takes its closing clause of those who caused the wrongs rather than those who suffered them; Keil and Delitzsch supply the verses in their own rendering, the fatherless torn from the breast, the poor defrauded, the naked slinking away without clothes and bearing the sheaves while hungry, and the oil squeezed out between the walls.

debates.question: Whose corn is reaped, and by whom?

sides.position: the corn of the poor, reaped as it stands by the wicked, who do not trouble to steal it from the barn
the corn of the tyrant, reaped by the poor who then go without themselves
the harvest of whoever owns it, carried off by roaming plunderers who rob all alike, even their own brethren in iniquity

debates.question: Who are the wild asses of the desert?

sides.position: the beasts themselves, or the poor obliged to keep their company, with the similitude supplied by the Targum
the oppressors, lawless and fierce and greedy of prey
men living a predatory life in the wilderness, seizing what they find to keep their families

outliers: Clarke alone sets his own survey of a poor city district beside the verse on the groaning of the city.
Henry alone turns the unwatered winepress into a charge against employers, that masters who withhold meat and drink forget they have a Master in heaven.
themes: a harvest reaped for someone else
the naked drenched on a hillside
a child taken from the breast
oil pressed by men who go thirsty

13.pericope_label: They are of those that rebel against the light; the murderer riseth with the light, the eye of the adulterer waiteth for the twilight and he disguiseth his face, and in the dark they dig through houses, for the morning is to them as the shadow of death

schools.summary: Gill has the murderer rise before sunrise, when the early traveller is on the road and the labourer going out, and lie in wait in a cave or thicket for them, explains that the twilight the adulterer waits for is of the evening and not the morning since the whole night is wanted, reports that some take the digging through houses of the adulterers just named but thinks such steps neither safe nor necessary, since admittance is got more easily by bribing a servant, and refers that verse to burglars proper, and takes the last verse to mean that the morning is alike hateful to all of them, murderer and robber and adulterer and housebreaker together, what is pleasant to other men being to these the shadow of death.

Henry sets the figurative and the literal reading of the light side by side without choosing, either that they sin against the light of nature and of conscience, professing to know God while refusing to be governed by the knowledge, or that they have the daylight and choose the night as the better season for wickedness; he makes the class the worst of sinners on two grounds, that they sin wilfully against their own convictions and so add rebellion to the sin, and that they sin deliberately, with plot and contrivance and a thousand arts of concealment, forgetting that there is no darkness in which a worker of iniquity can hide from God; he notices how small the plunder of the murderer is, a little money or goods carried to market, so that he ventures his own life for what hardly keeps the victim alive and thirsts more for blood than for booty, and turns the industry of such men into a reproach to the slothful; and he reads the adulterer concealment as shame and fear together, since even the most impudent of such sinners do what they can to hide the thing.

Clarke makes the murderer a highwayman driven to the work by poverty and distress, who robs by daylight and murders for fear of being taken, so adding crime to crime, and turns housebreaker by night; he has the adulterer mark the house, wait impatiently for the dusk, go out muffled, and then find the dawn terrible as the shadow of death lest he be recognised before he reaches his own door; and he supplies the housebreaking from his own time and place, thieves who dig through a mud wall and under a clay floor and plunder a house while the family sleeps; Wesley takes the light as reason and conscience together with the revelation then in good measure imparted, adding that not knowing its ways means not approving or choosing them, and gives the sense of the last verse in two words, that the morning is terrible and hateful to them.

Ellicott calls the phrase about rebelling against the light a very remarkable one which seems to anticipate the teaching of the fourth Gospel, offers the alternative reading of the second clause of the housebreaking verse, that they shut themselves up in the daytime rather than mark the houses beforehand, notes the custom still reported in eastern cities of gaining access to the women quarters in female dress, and observes that the order of the three crimes, murder and adultery and theft, agrees with the order of the Decalogue, which at least suggests acquaintance with it; Keil and Delitzsch render the whole series plainly, the murderer rising at dawn, the adulterer watching for the twilight and veiling his face, the walls dug through in the dark while they shut themselves up by day, and the depth of night serving them for morning.

debates.question: What is the light they rebel against?

sides.position: the light of nature and conscience, or else the daylight they avoid for their work; both readings stand
reason and conscience together with the revelation then imparted, whose ways they do not approve or choose
a moral essence, in a phrase that anticipates the teaching of the fourth Gospel

debates.question: Whose houses are dug through, and when are they marked?

sides.position: the houses of the rich, by burglars proper; the adulterers would not need such means, admittance being got by bribing a servant
houses marked in the daytime and broken into through wall or floor while the family sleeps
the clause may rather mean that they shut themselves up by day, as men still gain access in eastern cities in female dress

outliers: Ellicott alone notes that the three crimes are named in the order of the Decalogue and takes it as evidence of acquaintance with it.
Henry alone turns the diligence of these night workers into a rebuke of the slothful, that the sight should shame us out of negligence in doing good.
themes: sinners who shun the daylight
a murderer up before the traveller
a face muffled at dusk
morning as the shadow of death

18.pericope_label: He is swift as the waters, their portion is cursed in the earth, he beholdeth not the way of the vineyards; drought and heat consume the snow waters, so doth the grave those which have sinned; the womb shall forget him and the worm shall feed sweetly on him

schools.summary: Gill takes the first verse of yet another class of wicked men, pirates who rob upon the high seas, choosing the fastest vessels so as to run from place to place for prey and to carry off their booty when pursued, and who prefer that life to any husbandry on land; on the last verse he offers three senses of the womb that forgets, the mother or wife or friend, any of whom may bury him in oblivion either because his life was infamous or because his death was easy, or the womb of the earth in which he lies forgotten, or God himself, since the word carries the sense of mercy.

Henry gives the same reading of the first verse, with privateers cruising from channel to channel for prizes, and quotes a bishop of his own church for the gloss that such men despise the employment of those who till the ground and plant vineyards as poor and unprofitable; but he offers an alternative, that the words continue the account of those who fear the light, who make off quickly when discovered and lurk, not in the vineyards where they might be seen, but in some cursed portion, a lonely place nobody looks after.

Clarke renders the first clause literally, that light is he upon the face of the waters, and reports an emendation which makes it miserable rather than light; he fills in the picture of the snow water with the public tanks which had been filled by the snow melting on the mountains and kept for irrigating the land, and which the long drought had emptied, so that relief was cut off from that quarter as from every other, adding that the second clause is only two words in the original and that another reading makes them say that they fall to their lowest depth; and on the womb he takes the sense of compassion and presses it hard, that the line reads mercy shall be unmindful of him, exclaiming at the dreadfulness of a state in which mercy itself forgets a sinner and his perdition does not slumber, with the Chaldee turning the clause about the worms into a sentence on the cruel who neglected to commiserate the poor; Wesley reads the first verse of the man rather than his flight, that he passes quickly away with all his glory, like waters that never stay in one place, and will never again see or enjoy the vineyards he leaves behind, and keeps the plain statement of the last verse, making the breaking final since a tree once broken down never grows again.

Ellicott argues for the second reading of the first verse and against the comparison our version makes, holding that each of these rebels against the light is swift to escape over the face of the waters, that the cursed portion means a place men regard as of evil name, and that the man turns away from the frequented road through the vineyards and chooses lone and rugged paths instead; he sets the snow water against Job earlier speeches, where he had already spoken of a sudden death for the wicked as a blessing compared with the lingering torture he was himself undergoing, and reports a different construction of the last verse, that some read the whole of it as what ought rather to be the doom of the wicked, so that it becomes a wish; Keil and Delitzsch give their own rendering of the lines, drought and heat snatching away the snow water as the grave snatches away those who have sinned, and the womb forgetting the man while worms feast on him.

debates.question: Who is swift upon the waters?

sides.position: pirates and privateers, who choose the fastest vessels and despise husbandry on land
the rebels against the light, each swift to escape over the water and shunning the cultivated road for lone and rugged paths
the wicked man himself, who passes away with all his glory like water that never stays in one place
the clause reads literally that light is he upon the face of the waters, though an emendation makes it miserable

debates.question: Is the forgetting of the wicked man stated or wished?

sides.position: stated; the womb forgets him and the breaking is final, since a tree once broken down never grows again
some read the verse as a wish, what ought rather to be the doom of the wicked
the word is compassion, so the line says that mercy shall be unmindful of him

outliers: Clarke alone makes the verse say that mercy itself forgets the sinner, and stops to exclaim at the dreadfulness of such a state.
Ellicott alone reports a construction that turns the whole sentence from a prediction into a wish.
themes: a fugitive over open water
cisterns emptied by drought
a mother who forgets her son
a tree broken beyond recovery

21.pericope_label: He evil entreateth the barren that beareth not and doeth not good to the widow; he draweth also the mighty with his power, and though it be given him to be in safety, his eyes are upon their ways; they are exalted for a little while but are gone and brought low, and if it be not so now, who will make me a liar

schools.summary: Gill takes the verb about the barren woman as it stands and applies it to a man who upbraids a barren wife and is churlish to her on that account; he makes the oppressor the subject of the next verse, attacking men nearly as powerful as himself and drawing them by force or policy into his own acts of violence, and then takes the following verse the other way, that it is God who gives the wicked man to be in safety, so that he is preserved from the depredations of others and dwells secure.

Henry agrees on the barren woman and compares the upbraiding of Hannah by her rival, done on purpose to make her fret, observing that the childless, like the fatherless, are in some degree helpless, which is what exposes them.

Clarke reverses the first line, holding that the original should be rendered he feedeth, as the Latin took it, so that the charge is not cruelty to the barren woman but a selective kindness, the man having provided for her while leaving the widow uncomforted, being an enemy to the procreation of children and showing no mercy to large families; he follows another commentator into a third reading of the next verse, that the man draws guards about him for his defence and then, in the midst of them, does not feel assured of his life, which he calls an admirable delineation of the inquietudes of a tyrant, and carries that reading into the verse after, where the guards are given him for security and he leans on them while his eyes are on their ways, watching his own protectors lest they plot against him; of the end of such men he says that God puts down one and raises up another, and adds the historical observation that few tyrants reach the eternal world by a dry death rather than a violent one, and that all eastern history is full of it; and on the closing challenge he holds that Job has proved by examples that the righteous are often oppressed and the wicked often triumph, and defies his friends to find a flaw in the argument, adding the comment on the whole debate that neither side could hit on the middle way, which is that the wicked man may be in prosperity and yet miserable in his soul, and the righteous man in adversity and yet happy in his God, in which respects the ways of God are always equal; Wesley gives the reason the upbraiding stings, that barrenness was counted a curse and a reproach so that the man added affliction to the afflicted, and puts the safety with a warning attached, that God gives them these strange successes and yet observes them all and will punish in due time.

Ellicott keeps the tyrant as subject of the drawing but makes it moral, a great man pulling others after him by influence and example so completely that no one under his sway is sure of his life, offers a different construction of the safety, that each of his victims pays him tribute to be left secure while the tyrant eye is on all their ways, but grants that making God the subject, who gives the wicked man his security, makes very good sense too; and he reads the closing challenge as a claim about evidence, that Job has facts of his own as ready and as incontrovertible as those of his friends, and yet irreconcilable with theirs; Keil and Delitzsch render the closing lines plainly, the safety given and the eyes upon their ways, the exaltation for a little while, and the challenge that follows.

debates.question: Does he ill-treat the barren woman or feed her?

sides.position: ill-treat her, upbraiding a barren wife and adding affliction to the afflicted
feed her; the verb should be rendered he feedeth, so the charge is a selective kindness that left the widow uncomforted

debates.question: Who gives the wicked man his safety?

sides.position: God, who gives the wicked man to be in safety and yet keeps his eyes on their ways
his own guards, given him for security, on whom he leans while watching them lest they plot against him
his victims, who pay him tribute to be left secure

outliers: Clarke alone turns the first line inside out, making it a charge of partial kindness rather than of cruelty.
Clarke alone states the middle way neither party in the debate would take, that the wicked may prosper and still be miserable in his soul while the righteous may suffer and still be happy in his God.
themes: a reproach added to a barren woman
a tyrant who fears his own guard
safety granted and watched at once
a challenge to find the flaw
